title: Tz-V-H
hookLine: mitzvah, a command; Hasidic teachers link it to tzavta, togetherness

lines: A GOOD DEED, OR A COMMAND?
cards: "Do me a mitzvah and grab the door." In Jewish kitchens, mitzvah can mean a good deed, a kindness, a favor. Helping an old man with his groceries: a mitzvah.
Showing up at a shiva house with a casserole: a mitzvah. But the word underneath is sterner. A mitzvah is a command, something you're told to do.
A bar mitzvah or bat mitzvah is, word for word, a son or daughter of the commandment. So which is it, a favor or an order? Tzadi, vav, hey: Tz-V-H.
And a teaching that holds both.

teach.b: You met mitzvah on day six; today, its root. Turn it four ways. First, the order.
Tzivah means he commanded, and mitzvah is the thing commanded. In the Torah it's the language of instruction, not suggestion.
Second, the distance. Near the end of Deuteronomy, Moses says: "For this commandment which I command thee this day, it is not too hard for thee, neither is it far off."
And: "the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it." A command, here, isn't a weight lowered from above. It's close.
Some Hasidic teachers heard in mitzvah an echo of the Aramaic tzavta, togetherness, joining.

To them, a mitzvah is a point of connection: when a person does what God asks, the person and God are joined, for that moment, in one act. This is a teacher's play on sound, not a dictionary's history of the word.
In Pirkei Avot, Ben Azzai teaches that one mitzvah draws another after it.

Do one, and the next is easier to see. Some readers see it between people too: the neighbor you helped with groceries is the neighbor you notice next week. So the kitchen and the sermon aren't far apart.
A mitzvah is a command, and in the Hasidic reading, a way of being joined.

how: Jews speak of the mitzvot as the commandments of the Torah, while in everyday speech a mitzvah often means a good deed; some Hasidic teachers connect the word to tzavta, togetherness, and describe each mitzvah as a moment of connection with God.

games.q: you're Moses near the end of Deuteronomy, describing the commandment to the people. what do you say about it?
o: it's in heaven, out of reach.
it's very near, in your mouth and your heart.
only the priests can keep it.
games.why: "the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it."

practice: Think of one good act that would be better done together than alone: visiting someone who's lonely, cooking for a family with a new baby, clearing a neighbor's walk, giving to a cause side by side.
Choose the act and the person you'd invite, and picture the two of you doing it, noticing what the doing together adds. If you pray, you can bring both names into the quiet.
